title: Rita of Cascia (1381–1457)
hookLine: a wife in a violent marriage who became a peacemaker, patron of impossible causes

cards: A convent in Cascia, in the hills of Umbria, in the dead of winter. A sick nun asks a visiting cousin for something absurd: a rose from the garden of her old home. The cousin goes, expecting snow and bare branches.
Tradition says she found one rose in bloom and carried it back. People still bring roses to that nun's shrine.
But long before the convent, her life had held harder things than a winter garden: a hard marriage, a murder, and sons sworn to revenge.

teach.h: A HARD MARRIAGE, MET WITH PRAYER.
teach.b: Start with the marriage. Tradition says Rita hoped to enter a convent as a girl, but was married instead, to a hard and violent man. The stories say she met him with patience and prayer, and that in time he changed.
A word of care here. Rita's story is not a reason to stay in danger. The Catholic bishops of the United States have taught plainly that no one is expected to stay in an abusive marriage.
Rita is honored for what came next. Next, the feud. Her husband was killed in a vendetta between families.

teach.h: A MURDER, AND SONS SWORN TO REVENGE.
teach.b: Her sons, the stories say, swore to avenge him. Rita prayed that they would not become killers, and tradition says they died of illness before they could carry it out.
Then, the peace. Alone now, Rita asked to join the Augustinian sisters in Cascia. Tradition says they would not take her while the feud still burned.
So she made the peace herself, going between the families until they were reconciled, and then the convent opened its door. Finally, the name. People call Rita the patron of impossible causes.

teach.h: NO WORD SHALL BE IMPOSSIBLE WITH GOD.
teach.b: In Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, the angel tells Mary, "no word shall be impossible with God."
Rita's life is read as that verse lived out: a blood feud ended by a widow who had every reason to keep it going. The rose in the snow is the small sign. The reconciled families are the real one.

how: Catholics ask Saint Rita's prayers for situations that seem hopeless, and on her feast some parishes bless roses and give them to the people who come.

the rose in winter is a story from the Gospels
it's a story told about Rita. tradition says a rose bloomed for her in the snow.

games.q: you're Rita. your husband has been murdered in a feud, and your sons have sworn revenge. what do you do?
o: urge them on; the family's honor demands it.
pray they won't kill, and work to reconcile the families.
leave Cascia and never speak of it again.
games.why: tradition says she prayed her sons would not become killers, and later went between the families until they made peace.

practice: Name one situation that looks stuck, a family that won't speak, a diagnosis, a war on the news, a grudge of your own, and set it down in front of you without trying to fix it.

If you pray, hold it up with the angel's words, no word shall be impossible with God, or ask Rita's prayers; if not, hold it with care instead of despair, and notice whether one small step in it belongs to you.

wordCard.voice: Rita. A wife and widow who, tradition says, ended a feud between families and became an Augustinian nun; the patron of impossible causes. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: impossible causes. Peace came from the one with every reason to refuse it. Eight hundred thirty days now.
